article_title: Simple Solutions Learning – Standards-Based Math
citation: Simple Solutions Learning. (2025). Simple Solutions Learning evidence rating. https://www.simplesolutions.com
title: Supplement core instruction with short daily distributed review of previously taught skills to promote cumulative learning and retention
description: The article describes a design in which short, standards-aligned lessons revisit previously taught skills so that "the program's spiral structure is designed to strengthen recall and reduce learning loss by continually reintroducing previously covered content". Daily review of ten to fifteen problems in 10–15 minutes supplements, rather than replaces, the core curriculum. The evaluation associates this design with significantly greater assessment gains.
requirements: Daily implementation alongside the core math curriculum; teacher onboarding through professional development.
constraints: Evidence comes from one quasi-experimental study in grades 3–5; the design intent (retention, reduced learning loss) is stated by the program rather than separately tested.
target_learning_goals: Retention of previously taught math skills, procedural fluency, and multi-step reasoning
examples: Students completed ten to fifteen review problems per day, about 10–15 minutes, revisiting previously covered content.
key_sources: Simple Solutions Learning. (2025). Simple Solutions Learning evidence rating. https://www.simplesolutions.com

article_title: Literacy First – UT Austin
citation: Literacy First program description and evaluation summary. (2021). https://literacyfirst.org
title: Daily individualized tutoring sessions with response-to-intervention progress monitoring
description: The program's instructional design combines daily one-to-one tutoring with continuous data use. Tutors "work with their students daily in 30 minutes sessions that are tailored to address individual literacy/language needs," and the program is "data driven, with tutors using a response-to-intervention model that involves benchmark assessments and weekly progress monitoring." Attendance, fidelity, and implementation data are collected to inform both individualization and programmatic impact.
requirements: Trained tutors available daily for 30-minute sessions
Benchmark assessments and weekly progress monitoring instruments
constraints: Designed for students in kindergarten through grade 2 reading below grade level
target_learners: Struggling readers in kindergarten through grade 2
target_learning_goals: Individualized literacy skill development
examples: Tutors use benchmark assessments and weekly progress monitoring to tailor sessions to individual literacy and language needs

article_title: Developing and Enhancing Data Systems (In Focus Brief)
citation: Mathematica Policy Research. (2013). Developing and Enhancing Data Systems (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Design education data systems so they drive instructional and improvement decisions rather than drown educators in extraneous information
description: The brief argues that data systems should be developed and enhanced with decision use in mind, from the classroom to the central office and state education agency. It warns that "it is all too easy for data to leave educators and policymakers unmoved—or, worse yet, to drown them in extraneous information, rather than drive decisions that will improve classroom instruction, school performance, and student achievement." The brief therefore treats decision relevance as a core design consideration for data systems.
requirements: Data must be usable by decision makers and educators at any level of the education system
target_learning_goals: improving classroom instruction
improving school performance
improving student achievement
examples: The brief is one of a series offering recommendations and strategies for promoting effective data use by decision makers and educators.

article_title: A Participatory Approach to Designing a Student-Facing Dashboard for Online and Distance Education
citation: Herodotou, C., Shrestha, S., Comfort, C., Andrews, H., Mulholland, P., Bayer, V., Maguire, C., Lee, J. & Fernandez, M. (2025). description: The article argues that dashboards for online students should go beyond displaying descriptive performance data and offer prescriptive information — recommended materials to study and easy ways to contact tutors or support teams — so students can act to overcome performance challenges. Prescriptive data is described as of special significance to online students because it moves beyond describing their data to offering actions they should undertake.
requirements: Availability of actionable data such as material recommendations and support contact points
constraints: Prescriptive features depend on institutional capacity to generate recommendations and integrate contact channels
target_learning_goals: improving performance
study planning
seeking help

citation: Andrew Hegedus. (2013). Moving from data to making a difference. TASA INSIGHT Magazine 28(2), 17-21. https://www.nwea.org

citation: Crow, T. (contributing author Pipkin, H.). (2017). Micro-credentials for Impact: Holding Professional Learning to High Standards. Learning Forward and Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org/micro-credentials
title: Ground micro-credential selection in student and educator data so learning targets identified needs
description: Per the Data standard, educators should use multiple sources of student, educator, and system data — assessments, observations, attendance, demographics, behavior — to pinpoint needs before selecting micro-credentials, and use formative assessment and student work to monitor impact. article_title: Using Student Achievement Data to Support Instructional Decision Making
citation: Hamilton, L., Halverson, R., Jackson, S., Mandinach, E., Supovitz, J., & Wayman, J. (2009). Using student achievement data to support instructional decision making (NCEE 2009-4067). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. Retrieved from http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides/
title: Make data part of an ongoing cycle of instructional improvement
description: Teachers should adopt a systematic, cyclical process for using data: collect and prepare varied data, interpret it and form hypotheses about how to improve learning, then modify instruction to test those hypotheses. The guide advises that "not all instructional changes bear fruit immediately", so teachers should allow adaptation time before discarding an intervention. Teachers can begin the cycle at any point, including with a hypothesis or an instructional modification they want to evaluate.

Develop testable hypotheses that identify a promising intervention, a measurable effect, and comparison data

target_learning_goals: Adapting lessons, goals, and grouping in response to students' needs evidenced in achievement data
examples: The guide's testable-hypotheses box: teaching struggling 3rd graders the trade first method for subtraction and examining changes in their subtraction scores on the interim assessment, with pre-teaching scores as comparison data

article_title: Causal Inference and Bias in Learning Analytics: A Primer on Pitfalls Using Directed Acyclic Graphs
citation: Weidlich, J., Gašević, D., Drachsler, H. (2022). Causal Inference and Bias in Learning Analytics: A Primer on Pitfalls Using Directed Acyclic Graphs. Journal of Learning Analytics, 9(3), 183–199. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2022.7577
title: Use DAGs at the design stage of a study to decide which variables to control for and which to leave uncontrolled
description: The article recommends constructing a DAG before data collection so that decisions about when to control, what to control for, and when to avoid control can be derived by inspecting the graph. It notes that "statistical controlling for a variable requires that it has been measured in some way, highlighting the need for working with DAGs in the design stage of a research study." This principled approach replaces indiscriminate inclusion of correlated covariates, which the article calls garbage-can regression.
requirements: Variables considered for statistical control must be measured, so control decisions must be made before data collection
constraints: Statistical control's bias-reducing utility is proportional to the validity and reliability of the confounder's measurement
target_learning_goals: designing studies that support valid causal inference about learning interventions
examples: In the dashboard example, tracing back-door paths showed controlling for SRL would block both open paths while controlling for study behaviour alone would not

article_title: College Readiness for All
citation: Melissa Roderick, Jenny Nagaoka, and Vanessa Coca. (2009). College Readiness for All: The Challenge for Urban High Schools. The Future of Children. https://www.futureofchildren.org
title: Districts and states should build data systems that link high school performance to graduates' college outcomes and set validated readiness standards
description: The article argues high schools cannot be held accountable for college readiness without knowing what happens to their graduates: "districts and states will require new feedback systems that both provide schools information on the college outcomes of their graduates and link their performance during high school with their college outcomes." Readiness standards must be validated at performance levels giving students a high probability of accessing four-year colleges, show where students stand, measure progress, and give clear improvement guidance.

Readiness standards validated against outcomes such as credit-bearing course placement and degree attainment
Standards must allow districts to assess current standing, measure progress, and guide improvement
constraints: At present, no state uses its existing high school assessment system to benchmark college readiness, and only a few states have linked high school indicators to college performance
target_learners: High school students in urban districts, particularly low-income and minority students
target_learning_goals: College readiness measurement, college access, and four-year college completion
examples: The authors developed readiness benchmarks from Chicago data, identifying an unweighted 3.0 GPA cutoff using National Student Clearinghouse outcomes

article_title: Combining academic, noncognitive, and college knowledge measures to identify students not on track for college: A data-driven approach
citation: James Soland. (2017). Combining Academic, Noncognitive, and College Knowledge Measures to Identify Students Not on Track For College: A Data-Driven Approach. Research & Practice in Assessment, Volume Twelve, Summer 2017. https://rpajournal.com
title: Data-reduction framework combining decision trees, random forests, lasso, and factor analysis to prioritize college-readiness predictors
description: This framework uses data reduction to select, from thousands of measures, the variables that maximize classification accuracy for college enrollment and persistence. Decision trees recursively split on the variable maximizing information about the outcome using the Gini index, with mean reduction in the Gini index (MDGI) as a variable-importance measure; random forests replicate trees to counteract sensitivity to the first split, and lasso provides a regression-based alternative. A subsequent factor analysis (bifactor model) identifies what the retained predictors measure. The article uses it to show that "enrolling in college and persisting for a semester can be predicted with almost 90 percent accuracy using a small set of predictors."
requirements: A dataset with both predictor measures and recorded postsecondary outcomes, split into training and test data to protect against overfitting
constraints: Decision tree models do not generally account for measurement error
The methods maximize classification accuracy, not how actionable a measure is for educators
Findings need replication with newer data, as NELS predates grit and growth-mindset instruments
target_learners: K-12 and postsecondary students being screened for college readiness supports
target_learning_goals: Identifying students not on track for college enrollment and persistence
examples: NELS data from 12,144 students tracked from 8th grade in 1988 through 2000, with roughly 8,800 persisting for a semester as the outcome
key_sources: James Soland. (2017). Combining Academic, Noncognitive, and College Knowledge Measures to Identify Students Not on Track For College: A Data-Driven Approach. article_title: Responding to AI-generated emotional alerts: teachers' intervention and students' engagement in the mathematics classroom
citation: Osama Swidan. (2026). Responding to AI-generated emotional alerts: teachers' intervention and students' engagement in the mathematics classroom. ZDM-MathematicsEducation. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-026-01810-7
title: Dash4Emotion: a teacher-facing AI emotional alert dashboard
description: Dash4Emotion is a research prototype that gives the teacher real-time visual information about students' facially expressed emotions during problem-solving; students neither view nor interact with the interface. It classifies six emotions via a pretrained face-api.js TensorFlow model (about 310 KB, reported 70–80% accuracy on FER-2013), grouped into negative, positive, neutral, and surprise categories. An individual alert appears when a student exhibits a negative emotion continuously for at least six seconds, "displayed as a red-framed rectangle with the student’s name and an emoji"; positive emotions appear every fifteen seconds in green frames, and a class-level time-based histogram summarizes collective emotional states.
requirements: A standard webcam per student capturing facial expressions; the interface is teacher-facing only, with students neither viewing nor interacting with it.
constraints: The article states accuracy may decrease when participants wear glasses, precision in adolescent contexts may be limited because training data consist mainly of adult faces, the model was used as released without retraining or calibration, it cannot capture reflective or delayed states, and alerts served as cues for pedagogical reflection rather than definitive evidence of student emotion.
target_learners: high school students working on technology-supported mathematics tasks
target_learning_goals: making students' moment-to-moment emotional engagement visible to the teacher during independent work
examples: In the study lesson, red-framed individual alerts and the class-level histogram were synchronized with classroom video and used as temporal anchors for identifying analytic episodes.
key_sources: Osama Swidan. (2026). Responding to AI-generated emotional alerts: teachers' intervention and students' engagement in the mathematics classroom. ZDM-MathematicsEducation. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-026-01810-7

citation: Jarosław A. Chudziak and Adam Kostka. (2025). AI-Powered Math Tutoring: Platform for Personalized and Adaptive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12484
title: DAG-based course generation for structured learning and exam revision
description: The Course component generates an individual Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of relevant topics for structured learning such as exam preparation. The DAG shows prerequisite knowledge, suggests optimal learning paths based on textbook knowledge and dependency analysis, and enables students to monitor their learning progress. A pipeline of agents (Research, Planning, Step Handling, Coding) accesses memory and GraphRAG data to construct the structured DAG, which is stored in a database.

article_title: Alternative AI Philosophy: Daoism as Method for AI in Education
citation: Qin Xie. (2026). Alternative AI Philosophy: Daoism as Method for AI in Education.
title: Dao nature (道性) as epistemic aim for AI in education
description: Dao nature reconceives the epistemic aim of education in the AI era as ongoing attunement to a reality that exceeds conceptual grasp, rather than acquisition of fixed knowledge. The Dao is an undifferentiated, dynamic totality—"moving without end or exhaustion"—whose constancy is "the constancy of impermanence." Because AI remains a "black box" resistant to full explanation, the article argues educators should "acknowledge the boundaries of cognition and maintain reverence for that which cannot be fully known." Comprehending AI in education becomes a contemporary form of "cultivating reality" (修真), with each entity fulfilling the roles proper to its authentic being under Wuwei, non-interfering action.
requirements: A stance of reverence and incremental approach to truth under uncertainty rather than rationalist adjudication of good and bad in absolute terms
constraints: The article states careful contextualization is required to avoid Orientalism in translating classical concepts into contemporary educational contexts
target_learners: educators, learners, knowledge producers, and institutions in AI-mediated education
target_learning_goals: approaching truth incrementally under conditions of uncertainty; attunement to the complexity of AI in education
examples: The article reads the Daodejing's "Tao follows nature" (道法自然) and Wang Bi's gloss that the Dao "does not act contrary to naturalness" as the basis for treating the three AI challenges as instances of forced action (Youwei) rather than Wuwei
key_sources: Qin Xie. (2026). Alternative AI Philosophy: Daoism as Method for AI in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10842

article_title: Alternative AI Philosophy: Daoism as Method for AI in Education
citation: Qin Xie. (2026). Alternative AI Philosophy: Daoism as Method for AI in Education.
title: Daoist self-cultivation (修道) via Neidan as ongoing practice for AI in education
description: Self-cultivation is a sustained effort to align oneself with the Dao, transforming body, mind, and spirit. The article centers Neidan (Internal Alchemy), grounded in the Neiye's disciplines refining "vital essence (精)," "vital energy (气)," and "numinous spirit (神)," including "fasting of the mind" and "sitting and forgetting." Crucially, "There are no cognitive shortcuts: the practitioner cannot outsource this labor to external devices but must remain experientially and cognitively engaged." The Daoist self is relational, gender-inclusive, and free of age and class boundaries, making equality of access to learning an ontological given rather than merely an ethical injunction.
requirements: Learners and educators must preserve embodied, experiential engagement with reality; the whole person must remain cognitively present and ethically accountable
constraints: The article states surrendering cognitive agency to algorithmic systems as a thought controller stands in direct opposition to the Daoist project of self-cultivation
target_learners: all learners regardless of gender identity, age, ethnicity, or geographical origin
target_learning_goals: preserving cognitive agency and direct experiential engagement with knowledge in AI-mediated learning
examples: The article likens AI to "a refined implement, akin to the alchemical furnace or the herbal supplement, supporting but never supplanting the labor of interior cultivation"
key_sources: Qin Xie. (2026). Alternative AI Philosophy: Daoism as Method for AI in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10842

article_title: DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education
citation: Bang An, Maria Hamdani, Joseph Fox. (2026). DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19617
title: DataCanvas-EDU: a four-phase agentic framework for instructor-guided synthetic data generation
description: DataCanvas-EDU is an agentic framework in which the instructor specifies a teaching brief (business setting, learner level, permitted tools, assignment scope) and intended patterns through conversation, while an AI agent writes generation code, checks the exported data, and prepares reference analyses, assignments, and rubrics. As the paper states, "Four phases—Plan, Create, Verify / Test Analysis, and Evaluate—organize the process and support instructor review and revision." A shared case specification connects each intended pattern to its generation rule, comparison groups, measurement, and sample-size requirements, guiding checks and revision.
requirements: Instructor approval of the complete design before the agent begins routine programming and numerical checks; changes to a substantive pattern or its intended difficulty require the instructor's review
constraints: The current workflow generates records from scratch and its numerical helper supports Python generation and a single CSV table; code execution is subject to the host environment's permissions
target_learning_goals: data investigation and visualization
formulating analytical questions and justifying findings
examples: The paper illustrates the framework's Plan phase with a healthcare conversation example proposing four patterns for a four-site clinic network, and demonstrates the full workflow with the WindowDash case
key_sources: Bang An, Maria Hamdani, Joseph Fox. (2026). DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19617

article_title: Effects of extensive reading on reading attitudes in a foreign language
citation: Junko Yamashita. (2013). Effects of extensive reading on reading attitudes in a foreign language. Reading in a Foreign Language, 25(2). http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl
title: Day and Bamford's (1998) two models of L2 reading attitude formation and motivation to read
description: This article adopts two models proposed by Day and Bamford (1998), described as "the only ones currently depicting the relationship between reading attitudes and ER in the context of L2 reading." The acquisition model hypothesizes four sources of L2 reading attitudes: L1 reading attitudes, previous L2 reading experiences, attitudes to the L2 and its culture and people, and L2 classroom environment. The motivation model, based in spirit on Expectancy + Value models, holds that materials and L2 reading attitudes have primary importance in determining motivation to read, and the article uses the models to explain how ER may create a virtuous circle of reading.
requirements: The article states the models remain untested: "no study has ever attempted to test them," so sounder L2-specific theoretical frameworks are needed
constraints: The article notes the virtuous circle may not always arise because factors not affected by L2 ER, such as L1 reading attitudes, can also influence motivation
target_learners: L2/EFL readers, e.g., Japanese university EFL learners
target_learning_goals: Formation of positive L2 reading attitudes and motivation to read extensively
examples: The article interprets its finding that comfort increased more than practical value as consistent with the model's claim that positive attitudes enhance the decision to read

article_title: Motivation deficit in ADHD is associated with dysfunction of the dopamine reward pathway
citation: Volkow ND, Wang GJ, Newcorn JH, Kollins SH, Wigal TL, Telang F, Fowler JS, Goldstein RZ, Klein N, Logan J, Wong C, Swanson JM. (2011). Motivation Deficit in ADHD is Associated with Dysfunction of the Dopamine Reward Pathway. Molecular Psychiatry 16(11). https://doi.org/10.1038/mp.2010.97

description: The article proposes that ADHD involves not only attention deficit and hyperactivity/impulsivity but also motivation deficit reflecting "an hypofunctional DA reward pathway". The mesoaccumbens dopamine pathway projects from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens and is "critically involved in reward and motivation". Reduced D2/D3 receptor and DAT availability there, plus correlations between those PET measures and the Achievement scale only in ADHD participants, are offered as evidence that disrupted reward pathway function underlies lowered motivation and may contribute to inattention.

a trait motivation measure such as the MPQ Achievement scale

target_learning_goals: sustained engagement with tasks that are not inherently rewarding or reinforcing
examples: PET scans with [11C]raclopride and [11C]cocaine in 45 drug-naïve ADHD participants and 41 controls, correlated with MPQ Achievement scores

title: Diagnostic Analysis of Nonverbal Accuracy (DANVA) as a measure of adult facial and vocal affect recognition
description: The DANVA is the standardized instrument this study used to assess nonverbal affect recognition in adults, measuring "nonverbal facial and vocal affect recognition skills" through 24 adult face photos and 24 audio-taped sentence recordings, each depicting happy, sad, angry, or fearful emotions at two intensity levels. Participants view each face for no more than 5 seconds or hear each recording, then identify the emotion. Scores are error counts by channel, emotion, and intensity. article_title: Automatic coding of dialogue acts in collaboration protocols
citation: Erkens, G., & Janssen, J. (2008). Automatic coding of dialogue acts in collaboration protocols. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 3, 447-470. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-008-9052-6
title: Dialogue Act Coding (DAC) system: five communicative functions and 29 dialogue acts recognized via discourse markers
description: The DAC system identifies "dialogue acts", the communicative function of each utterance typed during online collaboration, building on the Verbal Observation System and discourse-analysis research. Its core assumption is that language users "signal the intended meaning and interpretation of their utterances to their discourse partners by means of explicit 'discourse markers'". It distinguishes five main communicative functions: "(1) Argumentative..., (2) Responsive..., (3) Elicitative..., (4) Informative..., and (5) Imperative (commands)", specifying "a total of 29 different dialogue acts". The system was used in CSCL studies of history and language arts inquiry tasks.
requirements: A limited set of discourse markers must exist in the language so they can be recognized by a computer system
constraints: The filter was designed for the Dutch language and requires translation work for other languages
The procedure only suits variables indicated by specific marker words, phrases, or actions, not more interpretive variables
The system codes most utterances in isolation, not taking preceding or following utterances into account (replies are an exception)
target_learners: secondary pre-university students collaborating online in CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: communicative functions of collaborative dialogue during inquiry tasks, including argumentation, responsiveness, and coordination of collaboration
examples: Table 1 shows a coded fragment of two girls and a boy collaborating on a historical inquiry task, with utterances coded as Inform, Respond, Command, Argue, and Elicit.

article_title: Ethnomethodologically informed
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2012). Ethnomethodologically informed. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 7:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9142-3
title: Validate interaction analyses through data sessions and multiple experienced analysts
description: Stahl proposes data sessions—involving multiple analysts reviewing the same data—as a mechanism for guarding against bias and idiosyncrasy in EM case analysis. Because the accountability of discourse makes it intersubjectively understandable, analysts sharing cultural understanding with participants can reach consensus on the meaning displayed. Detailed transcripts are published to allow reader validation.
requirements: Analysts must share the relevant cultural understanding with the discourse participants
constraints: Builds consensus rather than statistical generalization; suited to single or small sets of case studies
target_learning_goals: Collaborative learning: producing intersubjectively valid analyses of group meaning making
examples: EM case-study publications routinely include very detailed transcripts so readers can confirm the analysis from their own cultural understanding

article_title: Data to decision-making: how elementary students use their Community and Citizen Science project to reimagine their school campus
citation: Erin Bridges Bird · Heidi L. Ballard · Margaret Harte. (2023). Data to decision-making: how elementary students use their Community and Citizen Science project to reimagine their school campus. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09612-6
title: The data lifecycle: extending participatory science beyond data collection to decisions and action
description: The article describes the data lifecycle as the full arc of participatory science work, from developing expertise and defining research questions through collecting, interpreting, and sharing data to making decisions and taking action, then evaluating outcomes and reassessing goals. It holds that "data alone do not contain instructions for which actions to take" and that decisions are expressions of preference shaped by identity. The authors used it as an instructional design process for centering youth agency in their bird-monitoring CCS project.
requirements: Instructional designs must structure opportunities across all lifecycle stages, including expertise development, question definition, and data use for decisions, not only data collection
constraints: The article states the data lifecycle "does not provide instruction for how to make decisions about scientific practices or environmental decisions"
target_learning_goals: science learning through authentic data practices
environmental decision-making and agency
examples: The Ornithology Club project moved through expertise building on bird identification, designing an observation protocol, interpreting campus bird data, creating a Bird Sanctuary, submitting data to eBird, presenting to a Kindergarten class and the School District Board, and evaluating outcomes

article_title: Detecting Instruction Effects—Deciding Between Covariance Analytical and Change-Score Approach
citation: Köhler, C., Hartig, J., & Naumann, A. (2021). Detecting Instruction Effects—Deciding Between Covariance Analytical and Change-Score Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09590-6
title: Hypothetical data-generating model with trait and state components for diagnosing bias in instruction-effect estimation
description: The article proposes representing, via graphs, a hypothetical data-generating model containing all observed and unobserved variables affecting the outcome at T1 and T2 and the instruction variable. As the article states, "we use graphs to represent the state component, the trait component, their effects on the variables of interest (outcome at T1, outcome at T2, and instruction), and the instruction effect, denoted by δ". Researchers formulate assumptions about which components influence which variables, then deduce for which scenario the true effect δ is mirrored by the ANCOVA or CHANGE coefficient. Bias is defined as the difference between the true effect in the data generation and the estimated effects.
requirements: Researchers must formulate assumptions, based on apparent plausibility or empirical findings, about the presence of third variables and the relative sizes of trait- and state-specific influences.
constraints: The article notes assumptions regarding the model might not hold and alternative data-generating scenarios cannot be ruled out; interaction effects between instruction and the outcome at T2 were not considered and would make the model much less feasible.
target_learning_goals: unbiased estimation of instruction effects in two-occasion nonrandomized studies
examples: Applied to the DESI study, the Kunter et al. (2013) PCK example, the Holzberger et al. (2013) self-efficacy example, and the Lazarides and Buchholz (2019) teaching-quality example.

Reading matter that is relatively easy and interesting narrative
Explicit start and end points given to the group before reading

article_title: Addressing the theory crisis in statistical learning research
citation: Conway, C. M., Jenkins, H. E., Milne, A. E., Singh, S. & Wilson, B. (2025). Addressing the theory crisis in statistical learning research. npj Science of Learning 10, 68. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00359-6
title: Data–phenomena–theory framework with a bottom-up, phenomenon-driven approach to theory building in statistical learning
description: The article adopts Eronen and Bringmann's distinction between data, phenomena, and theories: "Data are the raw measurements collected in psychology experiments" and "Phenomena are a description of the effects compiled across the observed data", with theories created to explain and be constrained by phenomena. It advocates a "bottom-up" stance: before building theories, researchers should establish which phenomena are robust, validly measured, and causally understood, so that theories encapsulate only robust findings and avoid explaining unrobust ones.
requirements: Robust phenomena must first be identified using criteria of consistency, replicability, and detectability by several independent methods and observation approaches.
constraints: The article notes that development of any new theory of statistical learning is likely to be less clear and much noisier than the evolution example, and it is yet to be determined whether the reviewed phenomena are sufficiently robust for inclusion in an eventual theory.
target_learners: Researchers and theorists in statistical learning and the psychological sciences
target_learning_goals: Theory building grounded in robust, validly measured, causally understood empirical phenomena
examples: The article uses the theory of evolution as a model: Darwin's disparate observations (data) gave rise to general phenomena such as adaptation, competition, and heritability, which the theory of evolution by natural selection then explained and unified while remaining open to falsification.

article_title: Causal reasoning with causal graphs in educational technology research
citation: Weidlich, J., Hicks, B., & Drachsler, H. (2024). Causal reasoning with causal graphs in educational technology research. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10241-0
title: Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) as a graphical formalism for reasoning about causality and bias in educational technology research
description: The paper introduces DAGs as a visual, non-parametric tool for encoding causal assumptions and tracing sources of bias. It distinguishes DAGs from structural equation models, noting that "DAGs are non-parametric" and that "DAGs are conceptual tools" used for identification rather than estimation. The framework rests on three elemental configurations: forks (confounding), chains (mediation), and inverted forks (colliders).
requirements: Researchers must supply explicit causal assumptions from domain knowledge, since "there are no causal conclusions without causal assumptions".
constraints: DAGs are identification tools only; estimation is methodologically decoupled and requires separate statistical machinery.
target_learning_goals: drawing valid causal inferences from observational and experimental research designs
examples: The paper contrasts a DAG with a SEM: in a DAG, an arrow from X to Y asserts a causal effect without specifying functional form, whereas a SEM imposes parametric assumptions such as linearity and multivariate normality.

article_title: Teachers’ use of data from digital learning platforms for instructional design: a systematic review
citation: Alina Hase, Poldi Kuhl. (2024). Teachers’ use of data from digital learning platforms for instructional design: a systematic review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10356-y
title: Data use for teaching: a five-step circular process model
description: The review adopts Mandinach and Gummer's circular process of data use for teaching, in which teachers move from identifying problems and framing questions, through collecting and analyzing data, to deriving decisions and evaluating outcomes. As the review states, "We are following the data use for teaching process consisting of five steps: (1) the identification of problems and framing questions, (2) the use of data, (3) the transformation of data into information, (4) the transformation of information into decisions, and (5) the evaluation of outcomes." The review uses this model to frame how teachers turn platform data into instructional actions.
requirements: Data should not be collected without a specific goal; the process starts with identifying problems and formulating leading questions
constraints: The review notes transforming information into decisions seems to be difficult for teachers and is therefore often neglected
target_learning_goals: Using student data to inform instructional design and adapt teaching to student needs
examples: The review applies the model to interpret how teachers in the included studies moved from consulting dashboards to differentiation and individualization actions

citation: Sa’idah, N., Jailani, Sudiyatno, & Retnawati, H. (2026). Innovative teaching models and critical thinking in mathematics and statistics education: A meta-analytical review. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 12(1), 140-157. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijres.5054
title: Coded dataset of 19 studies comparing innovative versus conventional instruction on mathematical and statistical critical thinking
description: The article assembles a coded dataset of "a total of 19 studies" published 2017–2024, retrieved from ERIC, Scopus, and Google Scholar under PRISMA standards. Each record holds experimental and control group N, mean, and SD, the dependent variable (mathematical or statistical critical thinking), the independent variable (e.g., group investigation, blended learning, problem-based learning, metaverse technology), and educational level from elementary to tertiary. Table 1 summarizes the coding and Table 2 the computed Hedges' g values.
requirements: Studies must report critical thinking in mathematics or statistics as the dependent variable with experimental and control group sample size, mean, and standard deviation
constraints: Only two included studies measured statistical critical thinking; publications span 2017 to 2024
target_learning_goals: mathematical critical thinking
statistical critical thinking
examples: Table 1 codes studies such as Gaspersz & Salamor (2021, group investigation, college) and Rachmadtullah et al. (2023, metaverse technology applications, elementary) with group N, means, and SDs

article_title: Strategies for remediating clinical reasoning skill deficits in underperforming residents: a scoping review.
citation: Philip SJ, Cholifatul UF, Felicia CC, Nooreen A. (2026). Strategies for remediating clinical reasoning skill deficits in underperforming residents: a scoping review. J Educ Eval Health Prof. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2026.23.3
title: Daniel et al. clinical reasoning framework: seven domains grounded in illness script, dual-process, and cognitive load theory
description: The review adopts the clinical reasoning framework proposed by Daniel et al. as its conceptual foundation. The framework is grounded in illness script theory, dual-process theory, and cognitive load theory, and defines clinical reasoning as "a skill, process, or outcome wherein clinicians observe, collect, and interpret data to diagnose and treat patients." The construct is delineated into 7 domains: information gathering, hypothesis generation, problem representation, differential diagnosis, leading diagnosis, diagnostic justification, and management and treatment. The review uses these domains to align assessment and remediation with specific reasoning processes.
requirements: Educators must be able to identify precisely where within the reasoning process a learner's reasoning is breaking down for targeted intervention
constraints: The review notes that mapping specific remediation strategies to these domains remains challenging because several studies did not explicitly state the framework underpinning their interventions
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning for diagnosis and treatment
examples: The review aligns assessment methods with reasoning domains, noting think-aloud methods permit assessment across multiple clinical reasoning domains.

article_title: The Implementation of Data-Driven Assessment into Laparoscopic Skills Training: A Systematic Review.
citation: Hardon Sem F., Horeman Tim, Reijers Sophie J. M., Schoonmade Linda J., Daams Freek, van der Peet Donald L. (2025). The Implementation of Data-Driven Assessment into Laparoscopic Skills Training: A Systematic Review. Surgical Innovation. https://doi.org/10.1177/15533506251336824
title: Data-driven assessment tools as automated sensor-based systems measuring continuous variables representing technical skills
description: The review defines data-driven assessment tools as "automated sensor-based systems or devices that measured and recorded continuous variables that represented technical skills." These technology-enhanced tools use single or combined metric assessment, distinguishing them from non-automated methods like stopwatches, counted errors, or assessment forms. The review categorizes assessed skills into instrument handling (path length, speed, smoothness), tissue manipulation (maximum forces, mean force, force penalties), suture integrity (breaking strength, knot loosening), and anastomotic integrity (air pressure leakage).
requirements: Tools must be integrated into an existing skills course, training, or curriculum rather than used only in experiments or validation studies
constraints: Studies reporting only time to complete a task measured by stopwatch, counted errors, or assessment forms were excluded as non-automated
target_learning_goals: Technical skills assessment
Laparoscopic competency
examples: The most frequently used systems were LAP mentor, Forcesense, LAP sim, MIST VR, ProMIS, and Aurora

article_title: Differential attainment in assessment of postgraduate surgical trainees: a scoping review.
citation: Jones Rebecca L., Prusmetikul Suwimol, Whitehorn Sarah. (2024). Differential attainment in assessment of postgraduate surgical trainees: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05580-2
title: Four-theme, three-level explanatory framework for causes of differential attainment in surgical training
description: The review organises proposed causes of differential attainment into four themes identified from the included literature: training culture, experience of assessment, social networks, and personal characteristics. It then maps these onto Regan de Bere et al.'s three levels — macro (high-level policy), meso (institutional or working environments) and micro (individual factors) — stating these levels "can be used to more deeply explore each of the four themes to enrich the discovery of causes of DA". The framework is the review's own thematic synthesis, not a tested model.
requirements: Causes must be explored through qualitative research, which the review says is more attuned to capturing the complexities of DA than the predominantly quantitative performance-metric literature
constraints: The review states there is a paucity of data explicitly addressing why DA occurs, so the framework rests on suggestive rather than causal evidence
target_learning_goals: equitable assessment and progression in surgical training
examples: The review cites Ellis et al. on variation in training experiences and access to supportive peers and role models, Woolf et al. on trainee perceptions that relationships with feedback-giving colleagues could affect ARCP results, and Roe et al.'s protective factors such as supportive supervisors and peer networks

article_title: Construct-level predictive validity of educational attainment and intellectual aptitude tests in medical student selection: meta-regression of six UK longitudinal studies.
citation: McManus IC, Dewberry Chris, Nicholson Sandra, Dowell Jonathan S, Woolf Katherine, Potts Henry WW. (2013). Construct-level predictive validity of educational attainment and intellectual aptitude tests in medical student selection: meta-regression of six UK longitudinal studies. BMC Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3827328/
title: The 'dark variance' account of unexplained performance variance in medical selection
description: The article proposes that even after educational attainment's strong CLPVs (accounting for perhaps 65% of true variance in first-year performance), the remaining ~35% of variance — after measurement error, range restriction and right-censorship are taken into account — constitutes a 'dark variance' whose nature is not yet properly characterized, analogous to dark matter in astrophysics. The authors suggest some of it probably relates to factors unpredictable at selection such as illness or life events, and some to personality, motivation or study skills. This account sets a theoretical limit on any single selection predictor and motivates searching for additional predictor constructs.
requirements: A predictor (educational attainment) with CLPV substantially below one, so that remaining outcome variance must be explained by other, statistically independent constructs
constraints: The nature of the dark variance is not yet properly characterized; the article offers only probable candidate factors (illness, life events, personality, motivation, study skills) without measuring them
target_learners: medical students and medical school applicants
target_learning_goals: explaining variance in undergraduate and postgraduate medical examination performance beyond prior educational attainment
examples: The conclusion states educational attainment accounts for perhaps 65% of true variance in first-year performance, raising the question of the remaining 35%

article_title: The Relative Pedagogical Value of Disassemble/Analyze/Assemble (DAA) Activities
citation: Dalrymple, O., Sears, D. A., & Evangelou, D. (2013). The Relative Pedagogical Value of Disassemble/Analyze/Assemble (DAA) Activities. Advances in Engineering Education. https://advances.asee.org
title: DAA activities as reverse discovery: a discovery-based pedagogy that starts with the expert artefact
description: Disassemble/Analyze/Assemble (DAA) activities are described as an inherently discovery-based pedagogy that starts with the artefact, an instance of a typically well-engineered solution. Through systemized disassembly and subsequent analysis of components, students engage in an iterative process of observation and follow-up probing to understand component functions and their interconnection. The article frames DAA as overcoming a flaw of typical discovery activities, which tend to be unable to constrain students' explorations, by starting with the expert version. In engineering education, DAA is positioned as nurturing engineering thinking through interactions with artefacts.
requirements: Requires an artefact that is an instance of a typically well-engineered solution for students to disassemble and analyze
constraints: Both studies by the authors used a camera, a tangible and predominantly mechanical device; the authors state new types of engineering artefacts, beyond those that are predominantly mechanical and/or tangible, need to be assessed
target_learning_goals: understanding part-function relationships of engineered artefacts
transfer to novel design and diagnosis problems
motivation for engineering
examples: In the study, student teams of 3-4 systematically disassembled a Fujifilm QuickSnap Outdoor 1000 camera and recorded components and their functions, while the lecture presented the same content via multimedia PowerPoint

article_title: An Insight into a School's Readiness to Implement a CAPS Related Indigenous Knowledge Curriculum for Meteorological Sciences
citation: Alvin Daniel Riffel. (2015). An Insight into a School's Readiness to Implement a CAPS Related Indigenous Knowledge Curriculum for Meteorological Sciences. Universal Journal of Educational Research 3(11): 906-916. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2015.031117
title: DAIM pedagogical scheme for dialogical argumentation instruction
description: The Dialogical Argumentation Instructional Model (DAIM) pedagogical scheme is "a descriptive model arising out of the series of SKIP workshops" for enacting dialogical argumentation-based discourse, illustrated in Figure 2 and piloted successfully based on empirical evidence. During the two-month intervention the experimental group formed four randomized groups with rotating leaders and roles (reader, recorder, manipulator of apparatuses), presenting argument outcomes to the class. The article reports the scheme attained some level of cognitive synchronization among participants.
requirements: A teacher trained in the IKS/Science-based approach keeping content close to curriculum meteorological topics
constraints: Further procedural details were published elsewhere and are not repeated in this article
target_learners: Grade 9 learners in a previously disadvantaged community secondary school
target_learning_goals: Understanding meteorological concepts and developing argumentation and social skills
examples: The E-group intervention used a Conceptions of Weather questionnaire based on local indigenous knowledge, with group roles rotating each session

article_title: Using Video Feedback to Measure Self-Efficacy
citation: Linda Bobo, Amanda Andrews. (2009). Using video feedback to measure self-efficacy. Journal of Instructional Pedagogies. https://www.aabri.com/journal-of-instructional-pedagogies/
title: Dartfish Connect video feedback intervention with embedded written feedback
description: The educational intervention recorded students performing the psychomotor competency skill, digitized the video with Dartfish Connect version 4.5, and returned it on DVD with written feedback embedded in the video. The article states "The software used to digitize the video recording was Dartfish Connect version 4.5", an analysis software commonly used to assess body mechanics and skill performance. Written comments ranged from incorrect hand placement to incorrect patient positioning, and students were encouraged to view the DVD as many times as needed.
requirements: A scoring rubric shared between real-time assessment and video analysis for feedback reliability
A two-hour window for students to review the DVD before the second performance
constraints: Digitizing the video with Dartfish Connect took additional time, which the authors note may reflect computer capability rather than the software
target_learning_goals: performing an upper body neurological screening psychomotor competency skill
examples: Students were filmed performing the screening, the lead researcher embedded written feedback into the digitized video using the same scoring rubric, and students received the DVD before their second assessment.

article_title: The Power of Graphic Organizers: Effects on Students' Word-Learning and Achievement Emotions in Social Studies
citation: İlter, İ. (2016). The Power of Graphic Organizers: Effects on Students' Word-Learning and Achievement Emotions in Social Studies. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, 41(1). http://ro.ecu.edu.au/ajte/vol41/iss1/3
title: Daily graphic-organizer word-learning routine combining modeling, guided practice, cooperative construction and display of organizers
description: The experimental condition followed a recurring lesson routine: (a) modeling graphic organizers, (b) guided practice, (c) reading a selected textbook text, (d) generating comprehension questions, (e) filling in organizers with visuals, (f) using target words in clarifying sentences, (g) discussing word meanings, and (h) "hanging the organizers on classroom walls on which students can see and be proud of their products". Three organizer types were used: concept definition map, circle thinking map and word-questioning strategy, with think-pair-share for partner work.
requirements: One day of professional development for implementing the instructional practices, plus lesson plans aligned to the social studies curriculum scope and sequence
constraints: Implemented in 40-minute periods, three days a week over approximately 7 weeks in fourth-grade social studies
target_learning_goals: word-learning of social studies vocabulary, including definitions, examples-nonexamples, illustrations and sentence usage
examples: Students constructed organizers in pairs, generated sentences with each target word checked for semantic and grammatical accuracy, and presented organizers at the end of each lesson with cumulative assessment

citation: Thomas Rajotte, Christine Marcotte, Lisa Bureau-Levasseur. (2016). Evaluation of the Effect of Mathematical Routines on the Development of Skills in Mathematical Problem Solving and School Motivation of Primary School Students in Abitibi-Témiscamingue. Universal Journal of Educational Research 4(10): 2386-2391. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2016.041017
title: Implement daily routines of logical challenges or free practice of mathematical games to develop motivation and transformation-problem solving
description: The article recommends that educators embed daily mathematical activities in 3rd-grade classrooms: routines built on five types of logic challenges (Sudoku, chess, find an intruder, match replacing, Raven's matrices adaptations) or two hours per week of mathematical board games. The authors "firmly recommend educators to implement activities involving a daily routine of logical challenges or free practice of mathematical games", based on the motivation and problem-solving gains observed.
requirements: Activities are done on a daily basis (routines) or about two hours per week (games), over an intervention period of two months as implemented in the study.
constraints: Effects were demonstrated only on introjected extrinsic motivation and the transformation meaning of addition; the study could not generalize to rural third-grade children since no rural students were involved.

school motivation
examples: The first experimental group (N=48) did daily routines of five logic challenge types for two months; the second (N=33) played mathematical games two hours per week for two months.

article_title: Using Publicly Available Auxiliary Data to Improve Precision of Treatment Effect Estimation in a Randomized Efficacy Trial
citation: C. Z. Mann, J. Wang, A. Sales, and J. A. Gagnon-Bartsch. (2024). Using publicly available auxiliary data to improve precision of treatment effect estimation in a randomized efficacy trial. Proceedings of the 17th International Conference on Educational Data Mining. https://github.com/manncz/aeis-aux-rct
title: Data integration approach: auxiliary observational model predictions as covariates for precise RCT estimation
description: The data integration approach improves precision of randomized trial effect estimates by fitting a model on a large observational auxiliary sample to predict the outcome, then using its predictions on the experimental sample as a covariate. As the article puts it, "The predictions from this model, applied to the experimental sample, can be a powerful covariate for adjustment." Combined with a sample-splitting estimator for paired trials, the approach is unbiased because auxiliary predictions are pre-treatment covariates. The article also frames auxiliary data as a "sandbox" for flexible exploration without touching experimental outcomes.
requirements: The outcome of interest and covariates must be available for both the auxiliary and RCT samples, with overlap in characteristics and similar predictor-outcome relationships between the samples
constraints: The treatment need not be present in the auxiliary data, and the approach does not require correct specification of either model
target_learners: schools in randomized efficacy trials of educational interventions
target_learning_goals: precise estimation of the average treatment effect of an educational intervention on standardized test outcomes
examples: The article combined the data integration approach with a sample-splitting estimator for paired trials to re-analyze the CTAI study using TEA auxiliary data on nearly 3,000 Texas schools

article_title: Machine Learning-Based App for Self-Evaluation of Teacher-Specific Instructional Style and Tools
citation: Fedor Duzhin and Anders Gustafsson. (2018). Machine Learning-Based App for Self-Evaluation of Teacher-Specific Instructional Style and Tools. Educ. Sci. 2018, 8, 7. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci8010007
title: Data-Driven Classroom Tuning: a four-step methodology for instructor-led quasi-experiments on non-experimental score data
description: A methodology by which educators 'constantly improve their teaching by identifying teaching methods, instructional tools, and pedagogies that work best in their own classroom and acting upon findings'. It comprises four steps: flexible assessment letting students choose learning activities; acquiring an initial level of preparation (prior grades, pre-test, background data); predictive modelling of exam scores after the course ends; and matching the model's residual, called Added Value, to students' preferred learning activities. The article implements it with symbolic regression and a companion app.
requirements: The course instructor is free to select teaching methods, instructional tools, and pedagogies
There exists an objective metric measuring students' mastery of material when the course is over
Data on students' initial level are available and accurately predict the metric of students' success in the course
constraints: It is not a proper scientific method, at least not yet; the right statistical technique and group-selection method are unknown
It evaluates particular teaching methods rather than holistic pedagogies
Confounding factors not reflected in the chosen predictors are not eliminated
target_learning_goals: identifying which teaching methods and instructional tools work best in a particular instructor's course
examples: Quasi-experiment 1 compared clickers, handwritten homework, and online homework in ODE courses in 2015 and 2016
Quasi-experiment 2 compared team-activity measures against individual readiness assessments in a TBL calculus course

article_title: The Effects of Using Corpus Tools on EFL Student Teachers' Learning and Production of Verb-Noun Collocations
citation: Galip Kartal, Gonca Yangin Eksi. (2018). The Effects of Using Corpus Tools on EFL Student Teachers' Learning and Production of Verb-Noun Collocations. PASAA, Vol. 55. https://so04.tci-thaijo.org/index.php/pasaa
title: Data-Driven Learning (DDL): corpus-based inductive language learning
description: Data-Driven Learning is a pedagogical implementation of corpora in which learners work directly with corpus data. As the article defines it, DDL "helps language learners to observe and detect patterns and make generalizations related to the patterns they identified" (Johns, 1991). Concordancers, described as the most important computing tool for the approach, recover all contexts of an item and print them for rapid scanning and comparison. In this study, DDL was operationalized as student teachers searching verb-noun collocations in COCA and BNC and studying words in their contexts, supporting inductive learning of collocations.
requirements: Learners need access to a corpus with a web-based concordancing interface and a guideline on its usage before the experiment
constraints: Some students avoided concordancing programs because of technical problems or other reasons, per prior studies the article cites
target_learning_goals: verb-noun collocational knowledge and production in English
examples: Experimental-group student teachers signed up for COCA, studied words in context, and completed online collocation-searching tasks after class over four weeks

article_title: Teaching Interactive Art Lessons with Recycled Waste Materials as Instructional Resources
citation: Rita Yeboah, Eric Appau Asante, Nana Afia Opoku-Asare. (2016). Teaching Interactive Art Lessons with Recycled Waste Materials as Instructional Resources. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.14. https://www.iiste.org
title: Dale's Cone of Experience as the study's theoretical grounding
description: The study grounds its argument in Dale's Cone of Experience, described as "a visual device which summarizes Dale's classificat ion system for the varied types of mediated learning ex periences", organised as a progression from most concrete to most abstract experiences. The article cites the claim that people remember more of what they do (90%) than what they read (10%), and argues that making Art lessons practical with instructional resources should help students assimilate and retain more than hearing a lecture. Active learning and Multiple Intelligences theory are cited as additional grounding.
requirements: Lessons must incorporate active strategies and appropriate instructional resources so that learners use multiple senses in practical activities.
target_learners: Primary, Junior and Senior High School Art learners
target_learning_goals: Concrete, sensory-based learning through multiple senses
active engagement with learning material
examples: The article interprets the teachers' reports that resources made lessons more practical as reflecting Dale's Cone of Learning Experience

article_title: Graduation Coaching in a Rural District School
citation: Zeller, P. J., Carpenter, S., Lacefield, W. E., & Applegate, E. B. (2013). Graduation coaching in a rural district school. GEAR UP Learning Centers, Western Michigan University. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED555555
title: Use data-driven classification and visualization tools to proactively identify and monitor at-risk students for support interventions
description: The article recommends that schools use computer-based analytical and data visualization programs to proactively identify students trending toward academic failure and to monitor intervention effects, noting that "the data visualization and student identification tools discussed here are readily scalable to larger schools and school districts." With limited resources, "the selection process should be well-defined and reviewed on a regular basis to ensure equity within the program." These tools "produced changes in the ways in which schools assess, intervene, and support students."

A well-defined and regularly reviewed selection process to ensure equity
constraints: Coaching is a resource and staff intensive process; there are usually more identified at-risk students than resources for services
target_learners: at-risk middle and high school students
target_learning_goals: early identification of academic risk
equitable allocation of support services
examples: Classification dashboards built with SAS 9.2 and MS Access 2010 identified the 2010-2011 coaching caseload and provided quarterly formative feedback dashboards

article_title: Reading Achievement and Reading Efficacy Changes for Middle School Students with Disabilities through Blended Learning Instruction
citation: Jesse R. Pace and Daryl F. Mellard. (2016). Reading Achievement and Reading Efficacy Changes for Middle School Students With Disabilities Through Blended Learning Instruction. Journal of Special Education Technology. https://doi.org/10.1177/0162643416660837
title: Dane and Schneider's five-dimension framework of treatment fidelity
description: The article applies Dane and Schneider's framework of intervention fidelity, which identifies five dimensions: adherence, exposure, participant responsiveness, quality of delivery, and program differentiation. Adherence is "the extent to which specific program components were delivered as prescribed," while program differentiation "safeguards against diffusion of treatments." The authors use the framework to diagnose why the BELA blended learning evaluation failed to test the program adequately.
requirements: High levels of implementation fidelity across all five dimensions for an evaluation to adequately test a program's effectiveness
constraints: In this study, adherence and quality of delivery may have been unmet, per observers' notes
target_learning_goals: reading achievement
ELA skills
examples: Observers noted that at BELA1, blended learning activities were monitored by lab instructors rather than certified teachers who had received BELA professional development

article_title: A Study on the Mobile Learning of English and American Literature Based on WeChat Public Account
citation: Guiyu Dai, Yang Liu & Shanmeng Cui. (2018). A Study on the Mobile Learning of English and American Literature Based on Wechat Public Account. English Language Teaching, 11(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n6p47
title: Dale's audio-visual learning theory and Piaget's constructionist learning theory as the framework for WeChat literature mobile learning
description: The GDUFS WeChat literature program is grounded in two theories: "the audio-visual learning theory by Edgar Dale and the constructionist learning theory by Jean Piaget." Dale's learning pyramid holds that audio-visual-verbal materials function as more concrete experiences and that audio-visual methods of instruction can reduce forgetting and make learning more permanent. Constructivism holds that children learn best when they construct personal understanding through experiencing and reflecting, and the WeChat program can function as discussion forums, wikis and blogs enabling learners to actively construct knowledge.
requirements: Learning materials must employ verbal, audio and visual information together, as all 12 weekly articles do
constraints: The authors note Mayer (2004) and Kirschner et al. (2006) caution that purely hands-on or unguided constructivist activity may not produce real learning, recommending guided discovery
target_learning_goals: literary appreciation, interest stimulation, and knowledge construction in English and American literature
examples: The WeChat articles combine reading audio, short film clips, pictures, and text to arouse interest and make abstract literary content concrete

article_title: Corpus-Based Data-Driven Learning to Augment L2 Students' Vocabulary Repertoire
citation: Ira Rasikawati (2019). Corpus-Based Data-Driven Learning to Augment L2 Students’ Vocabulary Repertoire. International Dialogues on Education, 6(2), 83-98.
title: Data-driven learning (DDL) as inquiry-based inductive language learning
description: DDL, a term coined by Tim Johns (1991), is an inductive approach using computer-generated concordances that lets students act as "language detectives" or "researchers" exploring language data. The article grounds DDL in discovery/inquiry-based learning theory (Dewey, Bruner), noting that engaging students to discover language rules and patterns from authentic materials is central to inquiry learning. Johns's aim was "to cut out the middleman … to give the learner direct access to the data", emphasizing students' active role, the discovery nature of the method, and task authenticity.
requirements: Teacher guidance with discovery strategies so students can learn how to learn
Facilitation from teachers to investigate complex corpus data (Sinclair, 2004)
Collaborative selection of appropriate corpora, productive queries, and interpretation of data
constraints: Implementation of inquiry-based learning strategies can be context-bound depending on students' needs and learning goals
target_learning_goals: Discovering language patterns from authentic data
Learning how to learn
Generalizing linguistic rules from language examples
examples: Johns initially used DDL with his postgraduate students to improve their writing

article_title: Dynamic Assessment of Incidental Vocabularies: A Case of Iranian ESP Learners
citation: Sepideh Hanifi, Mahdi Nasiri, Hesamuddin Aliasin. (2016). Dynamic Assessment of Incidental Vocabularies: A Case of Iranian ESP Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 7(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.2p.163
title: Two approaches to DA: interventionist and interactionist
description: The article distinguishes two approaches to DA resulting from different interpretations of ZPD. The interventionist approach uses "a preset list of prompts and feedback for each item" and is described as psychometric-oriented. The interactionist approach "puts emphasis on learning over assessment," with mediational hints that are not scripted, requiring the examiner to respond to learners' needs throughout the DA procedure.
requirements: The interactionist approach rests on the examiner's preparation and understanding of the learner's ZPD

description: The article presents data-driven learning (DDL), introduced by Johns (1991), as the pedagogical approach in which learners work with corpora through concordancing software to identify regular patterns themselves. title: Daily 30-minute moderate-intensity running practice intervention
description: The core instructional element evaluated in the study: students participated in "running practice on the university's playground for thirty minutes each day over a period of four months" on a standard 400-meter track, at a moderate intensity aligned with WHO recommendations. physical activity engagement

description: The Devon Air Ambulance Trust programme is a bundle of educational and organisational interventions listed in Table 1 across 2018–2024. title: The 'data-case-simulation' trinity practice teaching model for interdisciplinary medical education
description: The article proposes a three-dimension practice teaching model organized around data, case, and simulation, in which students use open-source datasets for case analysis with clinical index modeling and statistical thinking. disease-centered bioinformatics and statistical analysis skills

title: Data Extraction Assignment: authentic assessment combining a literature data extraction table with multi-audience communication outputs
description: The Data Extraction Assignment, worth 30% of the final grade and completed over a suggested 9-week period, required students to select a dietary component and disease, summarize primary research articles into a data extraction table "to facilitate comparisons between scientific studies (worth 30 marks)", and produce three communication outputs: a two-page scientific summary (30 marks), a ~300-word plain language summary for a general audience (15 marks), and a pictorial summary/infographic (15 marks), followed by a rubric-based self-assessment and reflection (10 marks). citation: Servais Elliot L., Rashidi Laila, Porwal Priyanshi, Garibaldi Mark, Hung Andrew J. (2025). Novel force feedback technology improves suturing in robotic-assisted surgery: a pre-clinical study. Surgical Endoscopy 39(2):1217-1226. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-024-11472-9
title: Da Vinci 5 force feedback large needle drivers with console hand-controller sensitivity settings
description: The da Vinci 5 Surgical System (Intuitive Surgical) integrates force feedback instruments with built-in force sensors at the instrument tips that measure push or pull forces along the X, Y, and Z axes and relay them to the surgeon's hand controllers. The study describes instruments "similar in form and function to the standard instruments used in RAS, except for the addition of force sensors at the instrument tips". Feedback sensitivity can be scaled to three selectable settings ('Low', 'Medium', 'High'); the study set 'Medium' as the default and ran the non-FFB cohort with the setting at 'Off'. The instruments do not provide grip feedback or tactile sensation.
requirements: Force sensors at the instrument tips that measure push or pull forces along the X, Y, and Z axes and transmit them to the hand controllers
A robotic system whose hand-controller force-detection threshold permits sensing of relayed forces
constraints: The FFB instruments do not provide grip feedback or tactile sensation
Forces less than 0.5 N were excluded as the typical minimum threshold at which users detect forces at the hand controllers
target_learners: Novice surgeons (< 50 RAS cases in the last 5 years)
target_learning_goals: Suturing technique and force control in robotic-assisted surgery
examples: Twenty-nine novice surgeons performed seven specialty-agnostic suturing exercises repeated over four runs on dry models and ex vivo porcine tissue

title: DAS-guideline-based difficult airway simulation scenario set (CI and CICV) on Laerdal SimMom with standardized checklist assessment
description: A paired simulation scenario set for adult difficult airway training: a "cannot intubate, can ventilate" (CI) scenario and a "cannot intubate, cannot ventilate" (CICV) scenario, modelled on a Laerdal SimMom Advanced Patient Simulator with tongue edema to grade 4 Cormack and Lehane view, pharyngeal obstruction, and stiff lungs for the cannot-ventilate condition. Instructor-controlled digitally simulated EtCO2 and SpO2 physiology
A checklist instrument operationalising major protocol deviations per scenario
constraints: Simulated delays and distortions are unavoidable even with experienced instructors; fidelity does not replace real clinical experience
Choosing SimMom instead of SimMan (for obstetric scenarios and availability) could possibly affect performance
Scoring of improper equipment usage depends on instructor judgement

target_learning_goals: DAS protocol adherence in CI and CICV emergencies
correct selection and use of airway adjuncts and surgical airway technique
examples: In the study, standard settings included modelling tongue edema to grade 4 Cormack and Lehane visualization, with additional pharyngeal obstruction and lung stiffness for the cannot-ventilate scenario.

title: Dave's psychomotor taxonomy with Kolb experiential learning as an organising framework for online surgical skills teaching
description: The course organisers structured skill sessions around Dave's taxonomy, "progression of skills in the stages known as imitation, manipulation, precision, articulation and naturalisation", aiming to develop participants to articulation or precision. Within breakout rooms this was enhanced by Kolb and Fry's experiential learning cycle, "progressing from concrete experience to reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation and finally active experimentation". Breakout-room activities were mapped onto these stages: demonstrators asked students to instruct them to facilitate imitation, then supervised camera-visible practice with corrective feedback.
requirements: Learning objectives defined at the outset of each task
Demonstrators trained in teaching and feedback, briefed on marking schemes
constraints: The aim was development to articulation or precision, not naturalisation
target_learning_goals: Psychomotor skill development to the articulation level
examples: In breakout rooms demonstrators re-presented skills and asked students to instruct them, then delegates practised showing their model to the camera while demonstrators corrected technique

title: DART tool: a real-time quantitative debriefing assessment instrument based on cumulative tallies and ratios
description: The DART (Debriefing Assessment in Real Time) is a scoring tool developed at CAPE that "scores observable sequential debriefing contributions in a cumulative fashion including Instructor Questions (IQ), Instructor Statements (IS) and Trainee Responses (TR)". It requires minimal training and yields two ratios, IQ:IS and TR:[IQ + IS], intended to estimate debriefer inclusivity and participant engagement. It was designed as a real-time objective alternative to subjective Likert-scale debriefing assessment tools.
requirements: Raters tally instructor questions, instructor statements and trainee responses during or after viewing a debriefing; the two ratios are calculated from the recorded values
constraints: The article notes that with the advocacy-inquiry approach debriefers often mix statements and questions together, which could reduce reliability of DART scores and the inferences drawn about quality
target_learners: simulation faculty and debriefers in healthcare simulation education
target_learning_goals: improving debriefing facilitation quality and reflective practice in simulation-based medical education
examples: Eight faculty raters used printed paper copies of the DART to score two pre-filmed debriefing videos in real time and a transcript of Video A

article_title: Data-rich textbook figures promote core competencies: Comparison of two textbooks.
citation: Finby B, Heyer LJ, Malcolm Campbell A. (2021). Data‐rich textbook figures promote core competencies: Comparison of two textbooks. Biochem Mol Biol Educ. https://doi.org/10.1002/bmb.21488
title: Use data-rich textbook figures with authentic experimental data and no take-home message so students practice core competencies while learning concepts
description: The article recommends that instructional materials present authentic, unaltered research figures that students must interpret, rather than summary diagrams that state conclusions. It argues that "messy" figures with real data let students practice the process of science and quantitative reasoning simultaneously with learning core concepts, and that avoiding take-home message verbiage prevents inflated explanations that mimic comprehension.
requirements: Figures must contain results from real published experiments, not hypothetical or theoretical representations
Students must be required to analyze the item to extract meaning, with the take-home point not provided
constraints: Novice students may experience temporary frustration and discomfort when figures lack take-home messages
One semester was insufficient for data interpretation skills to persist six months later, per the authors' prior work
Data-rich commercial textbooks may limit access; the studied ICB is commercial, English-only
target_learners: AP biology and first-year STEM majors
target_learning_goals: process of science
quantitative reasoning
core concept understanding
examples: The authors compared ICB, whose integrating questions ask students to analyze and interpret published data, against Freeman's Biological Sciences across all 1598 figures and 226 tables
Think-aloud interviews used five paired figures on antibody response, endosymbiosis, hemoglobin, neuronal function, and carbon fixation
